section.title: Out of the Depths I Cry
section.sectionRationale: A Song of Ascents, eleventh in the pilgrim collection Psalms 120 to 134, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. Traditionally sung as pilgrims neared Jerusalem with cleared consciences, this psalm moves from the depths of guilt to the height of confident, waiting hope in the LORD's abundant redemption.
section.thesis: Out of the depths of sin and guilt, the psalmist cries to the LORD, finding not judgment but forgiveness, and waits for Him with a hope grounded in His steadfast love and plentiful redemption from all iniquity, a redemption fully accomplished in Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the cry from the depths, verses 1 to 2, the confession of universal guilt and the hope of forgiveness, verses 3 to 4, patient waiting for the LORD, verses 5 to 6, and the closing call for Israel to hope in the LORD's abundant redemption, verses 7 to 8.

units.label: Out of the depths I cry to You

verses.text: Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!
O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy.
If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?
But with You there is {{selichah|forgiveness}}, so that You may be feared.

units.label: My soul waits for the LORD

verses.text: I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope.
My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, more than watchmen wait for the morning.

units.label: He will redeem Israel from all iniquity

verses.text: O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is {{padah|redemption}} in abundance.
And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.

selichah.gloss: Forgiveness, pardon; a rare and warm term for God's willingness to wipe away guilt, given here as the reason His people fear and revere Him, not flee from Him, verse 4.

padah.gloss: To redeem, ransom, buy back by paying a price; the LORD's redemption of Israel from all iniquity is described as abundant and certain, verses 7 to 8.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents gives voice to a soul sunk in the depths of guilt, crying out for mercy, confessing that no one could stand if the LORD marked iniquities, and finding hope not in self-effort but in the LORD's forgiveness and abundant, promised redemption.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes one believer's honest cry from guilt to hope, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern honest confession of sin, patient waiting on the LORD's word, and confident hope in His forgiveness and full redemption, for the individual and for the whole people of God.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm moves from maamaqqim, depths, an image of overwhelming, drowning distress, to selichah, forgiveness, in verse 4, and finally to padah, redemption by payment of a price, in verses 7 to 8, tracing guilt's descent and grace's ascent in three key words.
basic.typology: The cry from the depths anticipates every sinner's cry for mercy answered in Christ, and the promise that the LORD will redeem Israel from all iniquity anticipates the full and final redemption accomplished at the cross.
basic.christ: The forgiveness this psalm marvels at, and the abundant redemption it promises, are accomplished fully in Christ, in whom believers have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, Ephesians 1:7, and who came to save His people from their sins, Matthew 1:21.
basic.god: The LORD hears the cry of the depths and is attentive to pleas for mercy, He does not deal with His people according to their iniquities but forgives, and He is the source of steadfast love and abundant, certain redemption from all sin.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 1:7 declares redemption through Christ's blood, the forgiveness of trespasses, the fulfillment of this psalm's hope. Titus 2:14 shows Christ redeeming a people for Himself from all lawlessness, echoing 'redeem Israel from all iniquity.' Matthew 1:21 names Jesus as the one who will save His people from their sins.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's cry from the depths, its wonder at forgiveness, and its hope in abundant redemption are all fulfilled in Christ, who bore the full weight of sin so that His people might be forgiven and redeemed from all their iniquities.

context.literary:
The psalm is eight verses in four couplets, and it is built like a staircase. The first couplet is all distance and noise: a voice crying from the depths, a petition that the Lord's ears would be attentive. The second is the hinge. Verse 3 asks a question no one can answer, and verse 4 begins with the small word 'But' and gives the answer no one expected. The third couplet slows to a vigil, and the fourth turns outward and speaks to the whole people.

The poet works with repeated words. 'Iniquities' appears in verse 3 and again in verse 8, so the psalm begins its argument with iniquities counted and ends with iniquities redeemed, and the words 'from all' make the second a complete answer to the first. The Hebrew preposition 'with' also carries the weight. 'With You there is forgiveness,' verse 4; 'with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance,' verse 7. What the sinner lacks in himself he is told is found 'with' God. The words for waiting multiply through the middle of the poem, and verse 6 repeats its comparison to the watchmen word for word, which is the poem's way of underlining.

The divine names are not used at random. The psalm moves between the covenant name, the title Lord, and the short form Yah in verse 3, as though the singer reaches for every name he has. And the verb of verse 3, 'keep track,' comes from the same root as the watchmen of verse 6, who keep their post. God does not keep a ledger of sins; the sinner keeps a watch for God.

It is also a psalm that widens. For six verses the singer says 'I' and 'my soul.' Only in verses 7 and 8 does the name 'Israel' appear. A private prayer ends as a public creed.
context.historical:
Psalm 130 belongs to the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, which pilgrims sang on the road up to Jerusalem for the three yearly feasts, Deuteronomy 16:16. A pilgrim arriving at the temple came to a system built around the reality of sin. Offerings for sin, guilt and consecration filled the sacrificial law, and the Day of Atonement set apart one day a year for cleansing the whole nation. A man who sang verse 3 while climbing toward that altar knew very well what he was admitting.

The image of the watchmen draws on ordinary life. City guards and temple watchmen stood through the dark hours, and for them the dawn meant relief and the end of danger. Isaiah 21:11-12 shows the same figure, a sentry asked how much of the night remains. In Jerusalem, dawn also brought the morning lamb on the altar, Exodus 29:38-39, and Psalm 134, the very next song, calls the servants who 'serve by night in the house of the LORD' to bless Him. A pilgrim near the end of the Ascents may have heard those night watches being kept.

The psalm does not name a date or author, and readers have placed it in several settings: a private penitent, a king, or the people after the exile. The deep-water language fits Israel's remembered rescues, as when the LORD 'made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over,' Isaiah 51:10. Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication also pictures the people confessing their sin in captivity and asking to be heard, noting 'there is no one who does not sin,' 1 Kings 8:46. Psalm 130 reads like that prayer put into song. Whatever its first occasion, Israel kept it as a song fit for the whole company of pilgrims.
context.canonical:
Psalm 130 stands in the old list of seven penitential psalms, with Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102 and 143, and the church has prayed it ever since at burials and in Lent under its Latin opening, De profundis. Luther loved it enough to turn it into a hymn. Its nearest neighbour in the Psalter is Psalm 143:2, 'Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You,' which prays verse 3 as a plea.

The psalm quietly rests on the great self-description of God in Exodus 34:6-7, where the LORD is 'abounding in loving devotion' and 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin,' yet 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.' Verse 3 feels the second half of that sentence; verse 4 holds on to the first. The prophets continue the same song. Micah asks, 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?' and promises that He will 'cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea,' Micah 7:18-19. The depths that swallow the singer in verse 1 become, in Micah, the place where God sinks the sins. Isaiah 55:7 says that the LORD 'will freely pardon,' and Daniel 9:9 confesses, 'To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him.'

The New Testament does not leave verse 3 unanswered. Paul explains in Romans 3:23-26 how God can forgive without pretending sin is small: through the redemption in Christ, whom God presented as the atoning sacrifice 'to demonstrate His righteousness.' The tax collector in Luke 18:13, beating his breast, prays the heart of this psalm in a single line. And Titus 2:14 takes up the last verse almost word for word, as Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted pilgrims to learn where to stand when they are guilty. The wrong places are easy to name. One is silence and hiding. Another is bargaining, the hope that our record is better than it looks. Verse 3 closes that door at once: if the LORD kept track, no one could stand. The right place is the one verse 4 names, with Him, where forgiveness is waiting before the sinner arrives.

He also meant the reader to see what forgiveness does. It does not produce relief alone; it produces fear, 'so that You may be feared.' A people who thought forgiveness cheap would drift, and a people who knew it was real would stand in awe. Then the singer teaches how to live between the prayer and the answer. The watchman's patience is not a mood but a discipline of looking toward a promise that has been spoken, 'in His word I put my hope.'

Finally, the closing call to Israel shows his purpose. He is not only giving one man's testimony but handing the nation a way to pray and a reason to hope together, since the LORD's redemption is larger than any single sinner.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records one voice in distress and what it found. It does not say that depths come to everyone in the same way, or that a person must feel a certain amount of anguish before God will hear. The 'depths' describe where this singer was, and the Psalter has other prayers from other places.

What it holds out as a pattern is the movement of the prayer: cry out, own the guilt without excuse, anchor hope in what God has said about Himself, and wait with expectation rather than despair. It is also worth noticing what the psalm does not prescribe. It does not tell the singer to earn forgiveness, or to wait for a mood of readiness. The forgiveness is already 'with' God, and the psalm tells us to wait for Him, not for our own improvement. Believers who read it today do so on the other side of the cross, so the waiting is for the full day of redemption, while the forgiveness itself is already declared, Colossians 1:14.

debates.question: Are the 'depths' of verse 1 only the guilt of sin, or a wider distress such as exile or suffering?

views.label: The depths of personal guilt
views.case: Verses 3 and 4 move at once to iniquities and forgiveness, and the cry of verse 2 is a plea for mercy rather than rescue. Sin's weight is described this way elsewhere, 'my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear,' Psalm 38:4.

views.label: A wider calamity that includes guilt
views.case: The Hebrew word for depths is used of deep waters in trouble of every kind, as in Psalm 69:2 and the sea of Isaiah 51:10. The closing verses speak of Israel's redemption, which could suit a nation in exile whose suffering is understood as the fruit of its sin, as in 1 Kings 8:46.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not rivals. In Scripture exile is never only political, and guilt is never only private. Either way the depths are met by the same God, and the psalm gives no hint that a sufferer must first sort the cause before praying.

debates.question: What does 'so that You may be feared' mean, and how can forgiveness produce fear?

views.label: Reverent awe
views.case: Fear of the LORD in the Psalms is the right response to who He is, not terror. Forgiveness shows a holy God who could have condemned and did not, and that is what draws a person to honour Him. This is the most common reading.

views.label: Obedient reverence in the covenant community
views.case: Some stress the practical side: forgiven people are to walk in the LORD's ways. Fear here is the settled loyalty that keeps a pardoned people from presuming on grace, since the God who forgives iniquity is still the God who 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished,' Exodus 34:7.

debates.bearing: Both views agree on the surprising point, that grace does not make God lighter. It is the very thing that makes a person want to live before Him. Paul faces the same objection and answers it in Romans 5:20 to 6:2.

debates.question: What is the 'word' of verse 5 in which the singer hopes?

views.label: God's covenant promise of forgiveness
views.case: The psalm has just cited the character God declared at Sinai, Exodus 34:6-7, and the hope in verse 5 rests on that self-revelation. The 'word' is what God has said about Himself and about redeeming Israel.

views.label: A priestly declaration of pardon
views.case: Others think the singer may be waiting for a spoken answer in the sanctuary, such as the priest's blessing, Numbers 6:23-27, or a prophetic oracle of comfort like Isaiah 40:1-2. The parallel with watchmen waiting for dawn suits a word expected at a particular time.

debates.bearing: The text does not choose, and a reader need not. Whether the word comes in the written promise or in a spoken assurance, the posture is the same: hope placed in what God has said, rather than in a feeling of being forgiven.

study.originalLanguages:
Five words and constructions carry the psalm. The first is 'depths,' maamaqqim, a plural form from the root for 'deep.' The plural is used for deep waters, the place where a swimmer loses his footing. Psalm 69:2 puts it as 'I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing,' and Isaiah 51:10 uses the same word for 'the depths of the sea' through which the redeemed crossed. So the opening line pictures a person underwater and shouting upward.

The second is the verb of verse 3, 'keep track,' from shamar, which means to watch over, guard or keep. It is the root used of keeping the sabbath and of the watchmen who stand guard. In verse 6 the watchmen are shomerim from this same root. The poem says that if the LORD guarded a record of iniquities, no one could stand, using the verb for standing in judgment as in Psalm 1:5, 'the wicked will not stand in the judgment.' Yet it ends with the singer as the guard, set on watching for the LORD. The verb of record keeping has been turned into the verb of hope. Another small point: in verse 3 the singer calls Him Yah, the shortened form of the covenant name, then Adonai, and the lines read as a rapid, urgent address.

The third is 'forgiveness,' selichah, introduced in verse 4 with the definite article, literally 'the forgiveness,' as though it were a known thing that belongs to God alone. A plural form of the same word is used in Daniel 9:9, 'To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness.' The clause that follows is easily misread. 'So that You may be feared' states a purpose: forgiveness exists so that awe will grow. The Hebrew verb is from yare, 'to fear,' the common word for reverent fear of God.

The fourth is the pair for waiting and hoping. 'Wait' in verses 5 and 6 is from qavah, the verb Isaiah uses for those who 'wait upon the LORD' and renew their strength, Isaiah 40:31, and which Psalm 40:1 doubles, 'I waited patiently for the LORD.' 'Hope' in verses 5 and 7 comes from a different verb, yachal, as in Psalm 119:114, 'I put my hope in Your word.' One word speaks of the stretching of the whole person toward something; the other of confident expectation.

The fifth is 'redeem,' padah, in verses 7 and 8. It is the verb of paying a price to release something that belongs to another. It is used of redeeming the firstborn in Exodus 13:13 and of a ransom no man can pay for his brother in Psalm 49:7-8. Hosea 13:14 sets it against death, 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol.' It differs from the other main redemption word, ga'al, which belongs to the kinsman redeemer. The Greek Old Testament renders the last verse with the verb lytroo, and Titus 2:14 uses the same verb for Christ, who redeems 'us from all lawlessness.' The same verb and the same sweep of 'from all' tie psalm to gospel.

typology.type: The depths and the waters, verses 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: Israel knew deep water as the place of death and also the place of rescue, since the sea was crossed on a road the LORD made, Isaiah 51:10. Jonah cried 'from the belly of Sheol,' Jonah 2:2, and was heard. Jesus took that pattern as His own sign, three days and three nights in the heart of the earth, Matthew 12:40. The escalation is that the Son went down for guilt that was not His, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The correspondence holds as a pattern of descent and rescue, but Jonah and Israel went down for their own sin, and Christ did not.

typology.type: The watchmen and the morning, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: The night vigil ends when the sun comes up. The women who came to the tomb 'very early in the morning,' Luke 24:1, and 'at dawn on the first day of the week,' Matthew 28:1, found the night of death over. The psalm's watchers wait for a morning that comes whether they sleep or not, and Easter is that morning for every sinner who waited for redemption. The type is not exact, since the psalm's dawn is God's forgiving presence in general, and the New Testament adds that believers still wait for the last morning, Romans 8:23-25.

typology.type: The price of redemption, verses 7 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Padah was the payment that set a firstborn or a captive free, Exodus 13:13. Psalm 49:7-8 admits that no human can pay it. Jesus said He came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and Peter says believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold,' but 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19. The escalation is from a price paid in animals and silver to a price paid in a life. It is also a payment that need not be repeated, Hebrews 9:12.

typology.type: The sanctuary where forgiveness is found, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: A pilgrim heading for the temple expected to find forgiveness at an altar. Hebrews says that Christ 'entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption,' Hebrews 9:12. Where the temple offered a cleansing that had to be sought again, the cross gives a once for all pardon, and believers draw near 'in full assurance of faith,' Hebrews 10:19-22. The picture falls short because the altar could cover sins for a year, while the work of Christ secures an eternal pardon.

study.christ:
Psalm 130 leads to Christ most directly by answering its own question. Verse 3 asks who could stand if the LORD kept track of iniquities. Paul gives the reply in Romans 3:23-26: all have sinned and fall short, and are 'justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,' because God presented Him as 'the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness.' This matters because the psalm leaves a puzzle. A holy God does not simply look away from sin, so how can forgiveness be 'with' Him? The cross is the answer. God stays just and justifies the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:26. Forgiveness that costs God nothing would make Him unjust; forgiveness that costs Him His Son makes Him both righteous and merciful.

It leads to Christ by the words of its last verses. 'He will redeem Israel from all iniquity' meets the angel's word to Joseph, 'He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21, and Titus 2:14, where Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.' Ephesians 1:7 and Colossians 1:14 use the psalm's vocabulary, 'redemption' and 'forgiveness,' almost as a pair, and say we have both in Him. The 'abundance' of verse 7 reappears in Paul's own words, 'where sin increased, grace increased all the more,' Romans 5:20.

There is also a pattern in the cry from the depths. Hebrews 5:7 says that in His earthly life Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence.' On the cross He prayed the opening of another psalm, Matthew 27:46. He went into the depths of death, not for guilt of His own, but 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. And because He was heard and raised, the watch ended in a morning, Luke 24:1.

The psalm also teaches how to hear the gospel. The tax collector who says 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' in Luke 18:13 is the person in verses 1 to 4, and Jesus says he went home justified. And because Christ 'is at the right hand of God,' and 'is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34, the one who hears the cry from the depths is the same one who can say that there is 'no condemnation,' Romans 8:1.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The psalm itself is a prayer of Israel's pilgrims and does not name a Messiah. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of this language and on the psalm's question, which only the gospel fully answers.
study.god:
The LORD of Psalm 130 is first of all a God who can be reached from anywhere. The singer does not climb to Him; he cries from the depths and trusts that the cry arrives. The petition that His ears be 'attentive' assumes a God who listens, not a distant ruler who must be persuaded to notice. And He is addressed by name, the covenant name, so the prayer rests on a relationship, not on a guess.

He is a God of searching holiness. Verse 3 does not say that the LORD does keep a record, but it takes for granted that He could, and that no one would survive it. The psalm's honesty is not pessimism about people; it is respect for who God is. The Bible does not offer a God who overlooks wrong, and the singer is not asking Him to. In the language of Exodus 34:7, He 'will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.' Everything in the psalm rests on that holiness.

Yet forgiveness is not an afterthought, a loophole in the character of God, but a part of who He is. 'With You there is forgiveness' says it is found in Him the way light is found in the sun. Daniel 9:9 says that 'compassion and forgiveness' belong to God. Micah 7:18 asks 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?', and answers that He 'delights in loving devotion.' Notice that the psalm names the purpose of this forgiveness as awe. God is not tolerating sinners; He is drawing them near.

He is also faithful to His word. The singer puts his hope in what God has said, and the last verses announce what God will do, not what He might do: 'He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.' This is a God who commits His future to His promises, who is rich in 'loving devotion,' hesed, and who redeems 'in abundance.' The amount matters. His redemption is not measured out in portions that match the sin; it overflows, as Paul says of grace in Romans 5:20.

There is a kind of tension the psalm lets stand. The same God is just and merciful, the one who could convict and the one who forgives. The Bible answers it in the end at the cross, but the Old Testament singers live with the tension and trust the character of God anyway.

For worship, the psalm shows how to come. We come without a defence and without despair, naming the guilt and the hope in the same breath. It teaches us to wait on God as watchmen wait for morning: certain it is coming, tired of the night, and unwilling to give up the post.

crossReferences.note: A close neighbour of verse 3 in the Psalter. 'Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You.' Where Psalm 130 asks who could stand, Psalm 143 pleads that God would not put anyone to the test. Together they show how Israel prayed over the weight of its sin and the need for mercy.

God's own description of Himself at Sinai after the golden calf, the foundation of verse 4. He is 'abounding in loving devotion' and 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin,' and yet will not leave the guilty unpunished. Psalm 130 feels both halves, fearing the second in verse 3 and clinging to the first in verses 4 and 7.

A prophet answers the singer's wonder. God 'pardons iniquity,' delights in loving devotion and will 'cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.' The same word for depths that held the singer under in Psalm 130:1 here becomes the place where God buries sin for good.

Another psalm that sets mercy against what we deserve: 'He has not dealt with us according to our sins or repaid us according to our iniquities.' It adds a picture of distance, 'as far as the east is from the west,' that gives verse 4 a measure.

Paul explains how God can forgive without calling sin small. The redemption in Christ, the atoning sacrifice through His blood, shows God's righteousness and justifies those who believe. It answers the question of verse 3 about who could stand: those who stand in Christ.

The tax collector at a distance, who will not lift his eyes and prays 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' Jesus says he went home justified. He lives out verses 1 to 4 and shows that the psalm's simple, unprotected cry is the kind of prayer God hears.

Another waiting psalm with the same verb for waiting as Psalm 130:5. The singer 'waited patiently for the LORD' and was lifted 'from the pit of despair.' It gives the outcome that Psalm 130 trusts without yet describing: the one who waits is heard and brought up.

A watchman is asked, 'what is left of the night?' and answers that morning comes but night also. It shows the watching image in its everyday use and reminds us that waiting for morning may take longer than the watchers hope, which is why Psalm 130 repeats the line.

The reason redemption needs God. No man can pay a ransom for his brother, because the cost of a soul is too high. Using the same family of words as Psalm 130:7-8, it states the problem that the psalm's last verses announce God will solve.

Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.' The verse takes up the language of Psalm 130:8, redeeming from all iniquities, and says who pays the price and what a redeemed people become: a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.

The LORD says, 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death.' It carries the verb of Psalm 130:7-8 into the face of death itself, showing that the redemption promised to Israel reaches past forgiveness to the grave.

Paul writes that in Christ 'we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace.' Redemption and forgiveness, the two great words of the psalm, are held together here, and the 'abundance' of verse 7 becomes the 'riches' of grace.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward, the Bible's story is the story of people who hid, were found and were asked 'Where are you?' Psalm 130 is what it sounds like when one of them does not hide. It is a cry from the depths, which the Bible has pictured since the flood and the Red Sea as the place where creatures go under, and from which only God can lift them. The psalm sits at the point where the Old Testament has long taught that God is 'forgiving iniquity' but has not yet shown at what cost.

It answers the great problem raised in Genesis 3 and Exodus 34. Since the fall, humanity has not been able to stand before a holy God. At Sinai the LORD described Himself as forgiving and also as just, and Israel lived in the tension: the sacrifices covered sin for a time, the prophets promised more, and the exile showed how deep the problem ran. Psalm 130 is Israel's best prayer inside that tension. It does not resolve it, but it refuses to give up on either half. It waits.

It also looks ahead. The abundance of redemption in verse 7 and the promise of redemption 'from all iniquity' in verse 8 are met when Jesus is named for the work of saving 'His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21, and when He gives Himself 'to redeem us from all lawlessness,' Titus 2:14. The night the watchers kept ends at an empty tomb in the early morning, Luke 24:1. Those who once could not stand are now said to be justified, Romans 3:24, and to have no condemnation, Romans 8:1.

The story is not yet finished, and the psalm's waiting still fits. Believers have the forgiveness now, but still groan 'as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies,' Romans 8:23. In the new creation the watch will end. There will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, and no curse, Revelation 22:3. The guilty one who cried from the deep will see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the God who did not keep a record will be the God with whom they dwell.

sermon.title: An Exposition of Psalm 130, Part One
sermon.why: Begg expounds Psalm 130 directly, encouraging listeners to follow the psalmist's example by crying out to Jesus for mercy in the depths of sin's despair and trusting Christ's sacrifice as the cure for iniquity.

quiz.q: Where does the psalmist cry from, according to verse 1?

options.text: Out of the depths, to the LORD.
options.note: This is the exact opening cry and image of the psalm.

options.text: From a place of comfortable ease.
options.note: The psalm describes overwhelming distress, the opposite of comfortable ease.

options.text: From the top of a mountain in triumph.
options.note: The image is descent into depths, not ascent to a triumphant height.

options.text: From a courtroom defending his innocence.
options.note: The psalmist does not claim innocence; he cries for mercy from a place of need.

quiz.q: According to verse 3, what would happen if the LORD kept track of iniquities?

options.text: No one could stand before Him.
options.note: This is the psalm's exact confession of universal guilt before a holy God.

options.text: Only the wicked would be affected, not the righteous.
options.note: The verse implies universal inability to stand, not a distinction sparing the righteous.

options.text: God would simply overlook minor sins.
options.note: The verse presents a serious reckoning, not casual overlooking of sin.

options.text: Everyone would stand except the psalmist himself.
options.note: The rhetorical question implies universal inability to stand, including the psalmist.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 say is the reason the LORD is to be feared?

options.text: Because with Him there is forgiveness.
options.note: This is the psalm's striking claim, that forgiveness, not mere terror, produces true reverence.

options.text: Because He punishes without mercy.
options.note: The verse ties fear of the LORD directly to His forgiveness, not merciless punishment.

options.text: Because He is distant and uninvolved.
options.note: The psalm portrays an attentive, engaged God, not a distant one.

options.text: Because His forgiveness is rare and unreliable.
options.note: The psalm portrays forgiveness as a settled, reliable characteristic of the LORD, not something rare or uncertain.

quiz.q: How does verse 6 describe the intensity of the psalmist's waiting for the LORD?

options.text: More than watchmen wait for the morning.
options.note: This vivid, doubled comparison is the exact image the psalm uses for intense, expectant waiting.

options.text: Less eagerly than a child waits for a meal.
options.note: The psalm describes waiting that exceeds even watchmen's intense longing for dawn, not a lesser degree of eagerness.

options.text: With complete indifference to the outcome.
options.note: The psalm's waiting is intensely expectant, not indifferent.

options.text: Only during the daytime hours.
options.note: The watchmen imagery specifically evokes nighttime vigilance awaiting dawn, not daytime waiting.

quiz.q: What does the psalm promise in verses 7 to 8 regarding Israel's redemption?

options.text: With the LORD is abundant redemption, and He will redeem Israel from all iniquity.
options.note: This is the psalm's climactic promise of full, abundant redemption fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: Redemption is available only for a select few sins.
options.note: The psalm promises redemption from all iniquity, not a limited selection of sins.

options.text: Israel must redeem herself through good works before God will act.
options.note: The redemption described flows from the LORD's initiative and loving devotion, not self-achieved merit.

options.text: Redemption will come only after many more centuries of waiting.
options.note: The psalm expresses confident, near expectation, not an indefinite postponement of hope.

questions: The psalmist cries 'out of the depths' rather than pretending everything is fine. What depths of guilt, grief, or despair do you need to bring honestly to God right now?
The psalm confesses that no one could stand if the LORD marked iniquities, yet finds hope in His forgiveness. How does resting in Christ's forgiveness change the way you deal with your own failures?
The psalmist waits for the LORD 'more than watchmen wait for the morning.' What are you currently waiting on God for, and how intensely are you actually watching and hoping for His answer?
The psalm promises abundant redemption from all iniquity, not merely partial forgiveness. Is there a particular sin or shame you struggle to believe is truly, fully forgiven in Christ?
This individual's cry widens into a call for all Israel to hope in the LORD. Who in your life needs you to share this same hope of forgiveness and redemption found in Christ?

translationNotes.note: Depths, maamaqqim, elsewhere pictures overwhelming, chaotic waters, as in Jonah 2:3, painting guilt and distress as a kind of drowning.
Forgiveness, selichah, is a comparatively rare Hebrew word, used only a handful of times in the Old Testament, underlining how remarkable and deliberate God's pardon is.
Redemption, padah, pictures a ransom paid to buy back something or someone from bondage, the same root behind the redemption of the firstborn in Exodus 13:13.
